parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what type of electromagnetic radiation can pass through the body but is absorbed differently by bone, soft tissue and air.
Hint 2: Think about why a normal X-ray photograph is limited - it flattens everything. How could you look at just one thin slice through the body instead?
Hint 3: One view of a slice is not enough to know where things are inside it. What would happen if you rotate the X-ray tube and detectors around that same slice and take hundreds of views?
Hint 4: You now have many different 2D shadow pictures of the same slice. How could a computer use all of them together to work out the detail inside the slice?
Hint 5: Finally, if you repeat this for many adjacent slices along the body, what sort of complete picture can the computer build up?
parts.proper_answer: CT uses X-rays. A thin section/slice of the object is scanned from many different angles to give 2-dimensional images of that section. Images of many sections are combined by computer to give a 3-dimensional image of the whole structure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start With X-rays**
Think of CT as a much smarter X-ray. You already know that X-rays are highly penetrating but are attenuated more by dense material like bone than by soft tissue. That difference in absorption is what creates contrast in the image.

Step 2: **Scan One Thin Slice At A Time**
Instead of imaging the whole body at once, the X-ray tube and detectors are collimated to look at just one thin cross-sectional slice. The patient is moved gradually so a new slice is studied in turn. This removes overlap from structures above and below.

Step 3: **Take Many Views Around The Slice**
The tube and detectors rotate around the patient. At each angle a 2-dimensional projection (a shadow pattern of transmitted intensity) of that same slice is recorded. So one slice gives hundreds of views from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$.

Step 4: **Let The Computer Reconstruct The Slice**
Each small volume in the slice, called a voxel, has its own attenuation coefficient. A computer processes all the angular data by back-projection and filtering to calculate the attenuation of each voxel and assign it a shade of grey. That is the 2D image of the section.

Step 5: **Stack Slices Into 3D**
The computer then combines the 2D images from all the adjacent sections. Put together, they form a full 3-dimensional image of the interior that can be rotated, sliced and viewed from any direction.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 10.2 as a summed, back-projected image. Each number there contains the true pixel value for that voxel plus several counts of the uniform background of 24.
Hint 2: In this 4-view simplified model, each summed value equals background plus three times the wanted pixel number. Think about how to isolate the pixel part first.
Hint 3: Try the arithmetic for the top-left voxel: subtract 24 from 42 and then divide by 3 to get K. Now repeat the same pattern for the other three positions.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Understand What Fig. 10.2 Shows**
Fig. 10.1 divides the slice into four voxels with unknown densities K, L, M and N. After viewing from the four directions $D_1$ to $D_4$, the detector data are added back onto each voxel position to give Fig. 10.2. In this simple model each summed number $S$ satisfies $$S = \text{background} + 3 \times \text{pixel number}$$ so you must remove the background and then share the remainder between the overlapping views.

Step 2: **Apply The Reconstruction Rule**
Background $= 24$. Rearranging gives $$\text{pixel number} = \frac{S - 24}{3}$$ This is the same for all four voxels, only $S$ changes.

Step 3: **Calculate K, L, M and N**
Top-left: $$K = \frac{42 - 24}{3} = \frac{18}{3} = 6$$ Top-right: $$L = \frac{45 - 24}{3} = \frac{21}{3} = 7$$ Bottom-right: $$M = \frac{30 - 24}{3} = \frac{6}{3} = 2$$ Bottom-left: $$N = \frac{51 - 24}{3} = \frac{27}{3} = 9$$ Larger summed values mean larger attenuation, so N is most dense and M is least dense, as expected.
